discussions.title: CW pump A's bearing in zone C: run it to the planned stop or stop it now

evidence.text: Zone C: not fit for long-term running. The machine may run for a limited time until there is a suitable chance to put it right.
Once a failure can be seen coming, the time left is the P-F interval: check more often than that, and act before it ends.
Pump manual, troubleshooting: vibration rising from worn bearings: read the spectrum, check the alignment and the feet, replace the bearings.
Motor bearing temperature above 90 °C. The heat comes last, near the end of the bearing's life.
Vibration past 7.1 mm/s, the zone C/D boundary: damage from here on.
Site rule: a CW pump comes out for work only once the standby pump is running and proven.

positions.claim: Stop it now and put C on duty. Zone C is borrowed time, and the bearing only gets worse.
Run it to Saturday's stop with a reading every shift. The crew and the crane are booked for then.
Let the readings decide: if it is still climbing or the heat has started, it comes out now.

turns.text: A's motor bearing is in zone C, 5.6 at the drive end. I want it out today.
Saturday is four days off and the job is planned for it. Will it get there?
Depends on the trend. Last month it read 2.9.

options.text: Back stopping it now: the temperature is up as well

lines.text: The bearing temperature is up too. That's the end of the curve, not the start.
If the heat is in it, I won't argue.

options.text: Back running it on: zone C allows a limited time, with a reading every shift

lines.text: Zone C gives us a limited time. With a reading every shift we'll see it coming.
Every shift, and it stops the day it passes 7.1.

options.text: Ask for a fresh spectrum and the readings before deciding

lines.text: Before we decide, let me look at the spectrum and the bearing temperature now.
Fine, but we decide today.

outcome.text: Stop CW pump A now on the standby pump; its motor bearings changed under permit today

lines.text: Past 7.1, it's not a discussion. Stop it.

outcome.text: Stop CW pump A now on the standby pump; its motor bearings changed under permit today

lines.text: Heat as well. Take it out.

outcome.text: Stop CW pump A now on the standby pump; its motor bearings changed under permit today

lines.text: All right. Out today, C on duty.

outcome.text: Run CW pump A to Saturday's stop: a reading every shift and the bearings regreased running; the bearing change stays planned for the stop

lines.text: Every shift, then, and it stops the day it passes 7.1.

discussions.title: Condenser pressure transmitter 2: calibrate it in place or at the bench

evidence.text: A two-point sensor trim against a reference at least three times as accurate, checked at five points rising and falling.
Transmitter manual, calibration: an absolute transmitter's zero needs a vacuum reference; one that keeps needing a large trim is drifting: replace its sensor module.
Transmitter manual: the sensor module and the electronics are changed at the workshop bench, the transmitter removed.
Transmitter 2 within 0.3 kPa of the true pressure.
Site rule: a trip transmitter is out of service for one shift at most, with the control room told and the trip vote watched.

positions.claim: Take it to the bench. It needed a big trim last month too: that's drift, and the bench has a proper reference.
Do it in place. It's one of three on the vacuum trip: the shorter it's out, the better.
Either works. In place is an hour with the hand pump; the bench is half a shift with the removal.

turns.text: Transmitter 2 reads 1.2 kPa above the other two again, a month after its trim.
It's one of the trip transmitters. Whatever you do, keep it short.
I can trim it in place this morning, or take it to the bench.

options.text: Back the bench: drift that comes back is the sensor, not the trim

lines.text: Trimming it again just hides the drift. On the bench we'll see if the sensor's going.
Then it's back before the shift ends.

options.text: Back calibrating in place: a two-point trim with the hand pump

lines.text: A two-point trim with the hand pump and the reference gauge will do, and it's back in an hour.
Then log the as-found. If it drifts again, it goes to the bench.

options.text: Check it in place first; the bench only if it is out of tolerance

lines.text: Let me check it in place first. If it's outside a quarter of a percent of span, it goes to the bench.
Fair. As-found on paper first.

outcome.text: Calibrate transmitter 2 in place: a two-point trim with the hand pump, as-found and as-left recorded

lines.text: In place, then. Record the as-found.

outcome.text: Calibrate transmitter 2 in place: a two-point trim with the hand pump, as-found and as-left recorded

lines.text: Within tolerance: in place is enough.

outcome.text: Take transmitter 2 to the I&C bench: removed, checked against the dead-weight tester, refitted the same shift

lines.text: Bench it, but I want it back before the shift ends.

discussions.title: CW pump A discharge valve leaks at its gland: tighten it live or isolate and repack

evidence.text: The packing seals the stem against the line's pressure; it is renewed with the pressure off, unless the maker allows otherwise.
Valve manual: repacking under pressure only on a gate or globe valve with a backseat, never on trip duty. Otherwise isolate and depressurise first.
Valve manual, troubleshooting: a leak at the stem is worn or loose packing: tighten the gland nuts evenly, or repack.
CW pump A running: the gland is under the pump's pressure.
The permit names the isolations; the work starts only once they are in place.
Site rule: no work on a pressure boundary, glands included, until it is isolated and proven at zero.

positions.claim: It's a weep at two and a half bar of water. A flat on each gland nut and it's done in ten minutes.
It's a pressure boundary. Isolate it and repack it properly.
It's a butterfly, no backseat. If the gland is near the end of its travel, nipping it up won't hold.

turns.text: A's discharge valve is weeping at the gland. Not much, a few drops a minute.
Onto the floor by the motor base for now.

options.text: Back isolating it: a butterfly has no backseat

lines.text: No backseat on a butterfly. Isolate it and repack it.
Fine. A out, C on.

options.text: Back nipping the gland up live

lines.text: The gland nuts have travel left. A flat each would stop it.
Not live. That's the site rule, however small the job looks.

options.text: Propose a sealant injection, done live by a specialist

lines.text: Could a specialist inject sealant into the gland while it runs?
Same rule. Nobody works on that gland under pressure.

options.text: Repack it today with new rings

lines.text: New rings today. It's an hour's job once it's isolated.

options.text: A drip tray now, then isolate it and fit live-loaded packing

lines.text: A tray under it now. Then we isolate it and fit live-loaded packing, so it won't need nipping up again.

outcome.text: A drip tray and the leak checked each round first; then isolated and live-loaded packing fitted (spring washers on the gland studs)

lines.text: Tray now, isolate it for the live-loading. Nobody touches it live meanwhile.

outcome.text: Isolate CW pump A and its discharge valve now and repack the stem with new rings

lines.text: Isolated, then repacked. Raise the permit.

discussions.title: The steam turbine tripped on bearing 3 vibration: restart it or find the cause first

evidence.text: Find the root cause before the event can repeat; gather the data while it is fresh, before anything is reset or restarted.
Turbine manual, troubleshooting: vibration that jumps suddenly can be a lost blade piece or a rub: do not restart before the cause is found.
Turbine manual: after a trip the rotor coasts down and goes on turning gear.
Bearing 3 still above its alarm level.
No turbine trip still latched.
Site rule: after a protection trip the restart waits until its cause is written in the shift log.

positions.claim: Probe 3 spiked and the others stayed flat. It looks like the probe: restart and watch it.
Not before we know. Pull the trends for all eight bearings and check probe 3's gap first.
Dispatch wants a time back. The trends are on the screen if you want them.

turns.text: The ST tripped on bearing 3 vibration high-high. GT and HRSG are holding on the bypass.
Was it just probe 3, or did bearings 2 and 4 see it too?
Dispatch is asking for a time back.

options.text: Back a restart: only one probe moved

lines.text: Only probe 3 moved. 2 and 4 stayed flat. It looks like the probe.
Looks like isn't the same as is.
If it is the bearing, a restart wrecks it. Check the probe first.
All right, but quickly.

options.text: Ask for the trends of all eight bearings before deciding

lines.text: I'll put all eight bearings' trends up, the last hour before the trip.

outcome.text: No restart: probe 3's gap and wiring checked and the trends compared first, the cause written in the log

lines.text: Still high on turning gear. Nobody restarts it.

outcome.text: Reset the trip and restart, a portable probe on bearing 3 and a hold at each speed step

lines.text: Restart, then, with a portable probe on 3 and a hold at every step.

outcome.text: No restart: probe 3's gap and wiring checked and the trends compared first, the cause written in the log

lines.text: Find it first. I'll tell dispatch.

discussions.title: Cooling tower fan 7's vibration alarm keeps going off: change its limit now or through a change

evidence.text: An alarm's limit comes from its rationalisation and is documented; changing it is a managed change with the reason recorded.
A change to a protective setting is reviewed and approved before it is made, a temporary one too.
Fan 7's transmitter junction box found wet.
Fan 7's vibration above 6.3 mm/s now.
Site rule: alarm limits change only through a change request signed by the I&C engineer and the operations manager.

positions.claim: Raise it to 7.1 for now. The operators acknowledge it every ten minutes and it's hiding the real alarms.
Not without a change. The reading climbs when it rains: that's water in the junction box, not the fan.
It came in fourteen times last shift. Nobody looks at it any more.

turns.text: Fan 7's vibration alarm again. Fourteen times last night.
That's the one that climbs when it rains.

lines.text: It's hiding the alarms that matter. Raise it now and do the paperwork after.
Then it's a temporary change with a review date, written down.

options.text: Back a change request and fixing the junction box

lines.text: If it's water in the box, a higher limit just hides a real rise later. Fix the box.
Then fix it today.

options.text: Propose shelving it for this shift under the shelving rules while the change goes through

lines.text: Shelve it for this shift, logged, and fix the box meanwhile.
Shelved for one shift, not suppressed.

outcome.text: Leave the limit; raise a change request, and dry and reseal fan 7's junction box under permit

lines.text: Water in the box. Leave the limit and get the box fixed today.

outcome.text: Raise fan 7's vibration alarm to 7.1 mm/s now as a temporary change, reviewed in seven days

lines.text: Temporary, seven days, and I sign it.

outcome.text: Leave the limit; raise a change request, and dry and reseal fan 7's junction box under permit

lines.text: Leave the limit. Get the box fixed today.
